story: Detroit's high-school parties of the early 1980s danced to European disco, which locals called "progressive", and to synth-pop. The radio shows of The Electrifying Mojo played Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra next to disco and funk. Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson met at Belleville High School, about 30 miles from Detroit, where they were among the few black students. Atkins took the word techno from Alvin Toffler's "techno rebels" when his duo Cybotron, with Richard Davis, released "Alleys of Your Mind" in 1981. The three went to Chicago to hear Ron Hardy and Frankie Knuckles, and joined that dance music to the mechanical sound of Kraftwerk, reflecting post-industrial Detroit. Rejecting the formulas of Motown and R&B, they called their music "post-soul". In 1985 Atkins founded the Metroplex label and released Model 500's "No UFO's"; May's "Strings of Life" followed in 1987. In 1988 the British compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, compiled by Neil Rushton and May, set techno apart from Chicago house. In the early 1990s clubs such as Tresor opened in empty buildings in former East Berlin, and by 1999 the Love Parade drew a reported 1.5 million people.

disagreements: Start date: our record says 1985; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Techno?action=raw says "Techno emerged in and around Detroit in the first half of the 1980s" and dates Atkins' use of the word to 1981. 1985 matches the release of "No UFO's" ("generally considered the first techno production").

Place: our record gives Detroit only; the article's infobox gives "Mid-1980s, [[Detroit]], [[Michigan]], U.S. [[Frankfurt]] DE", and says German literature describes techno as "a style that emerged in 1990 and based on [[Chicago house]]".
